title: Exploring Structure and Properties of Diseased Coral Exoskeletons using Multi-scale Electron Diffraction Techniques
content: Scleractinian or reef-building corals play a crucial role in marine ecosystems by forming calcium carbonate (CaCO3) exoskeletons that provide structural support for coral colonies and habitats for diverse marine life. The calcified skeleton is nominally composed of aragonite, a crystalline polymorph of CaCO3, and has a characteristic hierarchical structure of densely packed fibrous crystals radiating from centers of calcification (CoC) [1]. Coral skeletons exhibit heterogeneity in chemical composition, as the aragonite crystal structure can incorporate low concentration inorganic impurities such as Sr and Mg. Additionally, heterogeneity is observed in aragonite grain orientation within their skeleton. Moreover, various crystallographic defects, including twin boundaries and planar defects, have been identified within or between grains [2]. Nonetheless, little is known about the nano- through atomic scale influence these heterogeneities and defects have on the exoskeletons’ mechanical properties. Further, although it is widely established that a rise in ocean temperatures and ocean acidification contributes to the loss of coral communities [3, 4], much less is known about the effect of diseases on the mineralized skeleton. Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease (SCTLD) is a highly virulent disease affecting Caribbean reef-building corals, causing rapid loss of tissue and high mortality rates, ranging up to 94% for more than 20 species [5].
